claims.text: The low-field magnetocaloric response and hysteresis of non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi alloys are governed by the degree of microstructural heterogeneity.
The as-deposited alloy has an ordered, single-phase hexagonal structure.
Rapid deposition imparts a significant density of grain boundaries, defects, and local structural disorder to the alloy.
The as-deposited alloy undergoes a sharp, first-order magnetostructural transition.
The as-deposited alloy exhibits a large but hysteretic magnetic entropy change.
The as-deposited alloy has limited heat-exchange rates.
Controlled post-deposition annealing reduces grain-boundary density and defect-related disorder.
Controlled post-deposition annealing improves atomic ordering without changing the retained phase.
Grain boundaries, defects, and local strain fields modulate the distribution of local magnetic exchange interactions.
A broad distribution of exchange interactions caused by defects and local disorder produces an abrupt magnetostructural transition with high hysteresis.
Annealing relieves internal strain and minimizes chemical and structural variations, thereby homogenizing magnetic exchange interactions.
Homogenizing magnetic exchange interactions broadens the magnetocaloric transition.
Homogenizing magnetic exchange interactions reduces hysteresis losses during low-field magnetic-cooling cycles.
Annealing may cause a modest reduction in the peak magnetic entropy change.
The predicted broadening and hysteresis reduction apply at fields below 1 T near the magnetostructural transition.
The predicted effects require retention of the single-phase ordered structure and avoidance of secondary-phase formation.
The magnitude of transition broadening and hysteresis reduction depends sensitively on annealing temperature and duration.
